Which marketplace nets the most on this item?

Type one item once and see what it leaves you on ten selling channels side by side, after each one's fees. Free, no signup, and nothing you type leaves your browser.

The item

What each channel leaves you

Channel Fee rate Channel fees Net profit Margin Break-even price Price to match the best channel

Continue with these numbers

Each channel's own calculator opens with the item above already filled in. Nothing is uploaded — the figures travel inside this browser only.

    Adjust the fee rates

    These are editable defaults taken from this site's per-channel calculators, not a live fee schedule. If your statement says something different — a negotiated rate, a category this table does not carry, a promotional rate — put your number in and the ranking follows it. Leave a box blank to go back to the default.

    What each channel's number leaves out

      How to read this

      Every percentage here is charged on the whole order — the item price plus any shipping the buyer paid. Folding postage into the price to advertise free shipping does not avoid the fee.

      Marketplace fees are taken out of your proceeds, not paid up front, so they are not counted as cash you invested. That keeps margin comparable across channels that charge very differently.

      Subscriptions are spread over the orders-per-month figure you entered rather than ignored. That is what stops a $39.99 Amazon plan from looking free at two orders a month.

      A marketplace fee buys buyers. Your own store charges no referral fee and will almost always top this table on arithmetic — but it sends you nobody. Read that row as "what I keep on a sale I brought myself", and put the cost of bringing it against the difference.

      Which marketplace has the lowest fees? A worked comparison walks one item through six of the channels above step by step, including why the cheapest fee rate is not always the highest payout.

      Should I move off marketplaces to my own store? works the same item at five and sixty orders a month, and shows why your own store's lowest fee rate does not net the most until volume covers its subscription.

      Already selling and wondering whether you want connected analytics instead? This tool vs. Sellerboard sets a free pre-listing comparison against a paid, account-connected profit report, and says plainly what this page cannot tell you.

      Wondering why not just open each marketplace's own calculator? This tool vs. checking each marketplace separately walks through what goes wrong reconciling six tabs by hand, and what each channel's own calculator still does better.

      Need returns and shelf time in the ranking too? The where-to-sell calculator (it opens with the item above) ranks one item across eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Reverb, your own store, and a local sale after expected returns and what one listing is worth per month of shelf.

      Use it safely

      Everything runs in your browser. Your prices, costs, and volumes are never uploaded. We count only anonymous feature events in local storage (comparisons run, comparisons copied, and share links copied) — never people, content, IPs, or cookies. Counting honors Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control. Turn it off with the checkbox below. A share link encodes only the item, category, and rate fields in the page's URL fragment (after the #); a browser never sends that part of a URL to a server, so it is not sent to us either.

      Fee rates change. The defaults here were current when this page was written and are inputs, not a fee schedule. Confirm against your own statement before pricing a catalogue against them.

      No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

      Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

      Free and open source. If it helped you pick the right channel for an item, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

      Common questions

      Which marketplace has the lowest fees?

      It depends on the category and the price. Etsy's combined transaction and payment fee is about 9.5%, eBay's final value fee about 13.6%, and TikTok Shop's US referral about 6% — but Amazon and Walmart charge by category, from 8% on electronics to 20% on jewelry. On a $40 jewelry item Amazon takes about $8 and Etsy about $3.80; on a $40 electronics item Amazon takes about $3.20 and Etsy still takes $3.80. That is why this page asks for the category before ranking anything.

      Do marketplaces charge fees on the shipping the buyer pays?

      Yes, on all of the marketplaces compared here. The percentage is charged on the whole order — item price plus whatever shipping the buyer was charged. Folding postage into the item price and calling it free shipping does not avoid the fee, because the fee follows the total the buyer pays either way.

      Is selling on my own store really more profitable?

      On fees alone, almost always — an own-store checkout pays payment processing of roughly 2.9% plus 30 cents and no referral fee at all. But a marketplace fee buys buyers. Your own store sends you none, so that higher net profit only exists for a sale you brought yourself, and the advertising or audience-building that brings it is a real cost this comparison does not include.

      Why is Faire not in the comparison?

      Faire is wholesale. The buyer is a shop paying roughly half your retail price, and the economics turn on order size and reorder rate rather than on one retail order. Ranking it beside ten retail channels would produce a number that looks comparable and is not.

      Why is Whatnot not in the comparison?

      Whatnot is a livestream auction. Commission sits on the hammer and payment processing sits on the checkout total — the item plus buyer-paid shipping and tax — with published category caps a flat retail referral rate cannot express. Ranking it beside ten fixed-fee retail channels would produce a number that looks comparable and is not. The Whatnot seller payout calculator prices that split on its own terms.

      Why is Reverb not in the comparison?

      Reverb only accepts musical instruments and gear, where the ten channels above sell almost anything, so seating it in a general-purpose ranking would read as a recommendation to list any item there — which is true for none of the other rows' inventory. Its fee shape (a marketplace percentage plus payment processing) is genuinely close to eBay's, and the Reverb fee calculator compares the two directly on the same guitar or pedal, along with offer-versus-list, shipping, and return handling.

      How does the comparison handle Poshmark's $15 cliff?

      Poshmark keeps a flat $2.95 on any sale under $15.00 and 20% of the sale price from $15.00 up, so its fee is a cliff rather than one percentage: a $14.99 item pays $2.95 and a $15.00 item pays $3.00, while a $5 item pays 59%. This comparison prices that schedule directly, takes the commission on the sale price alone, and leaves postage out of both sides because the Poshmark buyer buys the prepaid label. The Poshmark fee calculator goes further with offer and bundle arithmetic around the $15 line.

      Can I share this comparison with someone else?

      Yes. "Copy share link" puts the item, category, and any rate overrides you typed into the page's URL after a #, and copies that URL to your clipboard. A browser never sends the part of a URL after a # to a server, so the item price and costs still never leave your device, just this one link instead of your typed retype. Opening the link loads the same comparison; nothing about it is stored anywhere but in the URL itself.

should-i-move-off-marketplaces-to-my-own.text:
Should I move off marketplaces to my own store?

Almost every fee comparison on this page ends the same way: your own store charges the least. That is true on arithmetic and it is not, by itself, a reason to move. Here is a $60 item worked through at two different order volumes, so you can see when the fee advantage is real money and when it is a subscription you have not paid for yet.

Compare your own item →

Five orders a month

A $60 home-goods item, $28 of landed cost, sold five times a month. Every channel's net profit after fees:

Channel Net profit
TikTok Shop$28.40
Mercari$26.00
Etsy$25.85
eBay$23.44
Walmart$23.00
Your own Shopify store$22.16
Amazon$15.00

At five orders a month, your own store nets less than five of the six marketplaces — not because its 2.9% payment-processing rate is high, but because the $39 Shopify subscription spread over five orders is $7.80 an order, and that dwarfs the rate advantage. Amazon has the same problem at a smaller scale: its $39.99 plan is $8.00 an order here, which is most of why it finishes last despite a referral rate no higher than Walmart's.

Sixty orders a month

Same item, same channels, same fee rates — only the volume changes:

Channel Net profit
Your own Shopify store$29.31
TikTok Shop$28.40
Mercari$26.00
Etsy$25.85
eBay$23.44
Walmart$23.00
Amazon$22.33

At sixty orders a month the $39 subscription is 65¢ an order, small enough that the 2.9% processing rate can do its job, and your own store moves from sixth place to first — $0.91 ahead of TikTok Shop, the next best, and $7.15 ahead of where it stood at five orders. The rate never changed. The volume did.

The number this table cannot see

Every marketplace row assumes a buyer who was already looking. TikTok Shop, Etsy, eBay, Mercari, Walmart, and Amazon all send you shoppers who arrived on their own. Your own store sends you nobody — the sixty orders in the second table had to come from somewhere, and whatever you spent finding them (ads, an email list, a following built elsewhere) is not in either table above. A store that nets $29.31 on paper and spends $10 in ads to generate that order nets $19.31, which may no longer be the best row.

That is why the comparison tool marks every own-store result with a note rather than simply ranking it first: the fee arithmetic is honest, and it is only half the decision. The other half — do you already have buyers, or are you about to go find them — is not a number this page or the tool can supply. If you do not know the answer yet, the safer read of both tables is "keep listing on the marketplace that already sends you buyers, and treat your own store as a lower-fee option for the customers who already know your name."

What moves the crossover point

Fifty-nine orders is not a rule; it is where these particular numbers happened to cross. Three things move it:

  • A higher-referral category moves it lower. On jewelry (20% at Amazon and Walmart) or clothing (17% at Amazon), the marketplace rows carry a heavier fee and your own store's 2.9% pulls ahead at a lower order count.
  • A cheaper Shopify plan moves it lower. This page prices the $39 Basic plan; a seller already committed to Shopify at a higher tier for other reasons has already paid the fixed cost, so the marginal decision looks better sooner.
  • Payment-processing surcharges push the other way. A store off Shopify's own checkout, or one paying a gateway a point above 2.9%, gives back part of the advantage this page assumes.

Run your own item and your own order count through the comparison rather than trusting the crossover point above — it moves with every input on this page.

Run the comparison on your item →

Fee rates quoted here were current when this page was written and are starting points, not a live fee schedule. Confirm against your own statement before pricing a catalogue against them.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. This is an arithmetic comparison, not tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-checking-each-marketplace-separately..text:
← Marketplace Fee Comparison

This tool vs. checking each marketplace's fee calculator separately

Six tabs, six retypes, six numbers to reconcile by hand — and the reconciliation, not the arithmetic inside any one tab, is where a seller gives up and guesses. This page runs one item through eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop, and your own store at once and ranks what each one actually leaves you, free and in your browser.

What each one is for

Every marketplace publishes a calculator scoped to its own fees, and on its own fees each one is the authority. It is maintained by the company that sets the schedule, it knows category exceptions, and it can see account-level terms — a store subscription tier, a promotion — that no outside page can. What it cannot do is rank, because it has no figure for what a different channel would have left you and no reason to produce one.

So a seller holding one unlisted item opens six calculators, types the same price and cost into each, writes six numbers down, and compares them by eye. That last step is the one this page replaces: type the item once, and every channel is ranked on the same model at the same time.

What you want to knowWhere to answer it
I have decided to list on this one marketplace. Exactly what will its fees be on my account, in my category?That marketplace's own calculator — it is the authority on its own schedule, and this page is not.
I am holding one item and have not listed it anywhere. Which channel leaves me the most?This tool — type the item once and every channel is ranked side by side on the same fee model.
Is a channel's monthly plan worth it at the volume I actually sell?This tool — it spreads the subscription over the orders you typed, so a low-volume seller sees the real per-order cost.
Does the category I am selling in change which channel wins?This tool — category is a required input, because two channels can charge very differently on the exact same item.
Do I need an account, a subscription, or a sign-in to compare?This tool: none of the three. It is a static page and the arithmetic runs in your browser.

Three things that go wrong reconciling six calculators by hand

Each of these is a difference between channels, and a single-channel calculator has no reason to mention a difference within its own channel it does not have.

Category changes the rate on some channels and not others

Two of the six channels compared here set their referral rate by product category; the rest charge one flat rate regardless of what is being sold. That means the same item can sit at a low rate on one channel and a meaningfully higher rate on another for a reason that has nothing to do with either channel's headline number — and a seller comparing headline rates from memory has no way to catch it, because the headline rate is not what the category-priced channel actually charges. This page asks for the category before ranking anything so that difference is in the comparison rather than hidden behind it.

A monthly plan is not a per-order fee

A flat subscription does not change with the sale, so it cannot be turned into a per-order cost without knowing how many orders the month will hold. At low volume it can be the largest single cost on the item; at high volume it rounds toward nothing. A calculator scoped to one order has no monthly figure to spread it over and either omits the subscription or attributes the whole month to the one item on screen. This page asks for expected monthly orders and amortizes every subscription across them, so a plan is compared as what it actually costs at your volume rather than at an assumed one.

The percentage is charged on the whole order, not just the item price

Every channel compared here charges its percentage on the item price plus whatever shipping the buyer was charged, not on the item price alone. Folding postage into the price to advertise free shipping does not avoid the fee — it is still charged on the total the buyer paid. A quick mental estimate against the item price alone therefore understates every channel's fee by the same missed amount, which cancels out only if every channel is estimated the same wrong way and does not cancel out at all once shipping charges differ between listings.

A fourth difference belongs here too, and it is covered on the tool itself rather than repeated in full: your own store almost always tops a fee-only comparison, because it charges no referral fee at all — and it also sends you no buyers, so that figure only holds for a sale you brought yourself.

What each marketplace's own calculator does better

The honest half of the comparison. On the question it is built for, a marketplace's own calculator beats this page, and a seller who uses only this one is missing things:

  • It is the current schedule; this page is not. The rates here are editable defaults that were accurate when the page was written, and they are inputs rather than a published fee schedule. Marketplaces change fees. The marketplace's own calculator changes with them on the day.
  • It knows your actual category and any exception attached to it. This page uses one rate per channel — the category you selected, or the number you typed over it.
  • It knows your account. A store subscription tier, a promotional period, a seller-level discount: all of that is visible to the marketplace and invisible here.
  • It can see your real orders. Some are wired into your actual listings and settlement reports. This page has no account, no connection, and no order history — every figure in it is one you supplied.

So the sequence that gets the most out of both is: rank the channels here while the item is still unlisted, then confirm on the winning channel's own calculator with your own account's rates before you set the price. This page makes no claim about any marketplace calculator's accuracy or current terms, and does not evaluate one — it describes only the shape of what each kind of tool is for.

No account and no sign-in: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded.

Common questions

Why not just check each marketplace's own fee calculator?

Each one answers a single channel completely and correctly: what will this item cost me here? None of them can answer where should I list this, because none of them has a figure for what a different channel would have left you, and no reason to produce one. Getting from six correct single-channel answers to a ranking means opening six tabs, retyping the same item six times, and reconciling six numbers by hand — and that reconciliation, not the fee arithmetic inside any one tab, is where a seller gives up and guesses.

What goes wrong when I compare marketplace calculators by hand?

Three things, and each is easy to miss when you are eyeballing rate cards rather than running the numbers side by side. Some channels price a category by a flat percentage; others set the referral rate by category, so the same item can sit at a low rate on one channel and a high rate on another for a reason that has nothing to do with the channel's headline number. A monthly subscription is not a per-order fee, so it only becomes comparable to a percentage once it is spread over the orders you actually expect that month — at low volume it can be the largest line item, and a calculator scoped to one order has no volume to spread it over. And every percentage here applies to the whole order the buyer pays, item plus any shipping they were charged, which a quick mental estimate against the item price alone will understate.

Is this page more accurate than a marketplace's own calculator?

No, and on its own fees a marketplace's calculator should be treated as the authority. It is maintained by the company that sets the fees, reflects the schedule currently published, and can see category exceptions and account-level terms this page cannot. The rates here are editable defaults that were current when this page was written, not a live fee schedule. What this page adds is not precision on one channel — it is one consistent model applied to all of them at once, so the numbers being compared were produced the same way.

So should I use both?

That is the honest order to use them in. Run the comparison here first, while the item is still unlisted, to see which one or two channels are worth the effort at all. Then open the winning channel's own calculator to confirm against your actual account — your real category, any negotiated or promotional rate, your store subscription tier. The two are sequential, not competing: a ranking across channels, then a confirmation on the one you picked.

Is this page affiliated with eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop, or Shopify?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any marketplace named on it. Those names are used only to say which channels the comparison covers and to describe the publicly documented shape of each one's fees. No marketplace's calculator is reproduced, quoted, or evaluated here.

Open the marketplace fee comparison to rank your own item, read which marketplace has the lowest fees for a worked example, or see this tool vs. Sellerboard for the difference between a pre-listing ranking and connected seller analytics.

Use it safely

Fee rates change. The defaults in the comparison tool were current when it was written and are inputs, not a fee schedule. Confirm against your own statement, or the marketplace's own calculator, before pricing a catalogue against them.

vs-sellerboard.html.text:
← Marketplace Fee Comparison

This tool vs. Sellerboard

Two different questions, asked at different moments. Sellerboard reports what orders you already shipped actually earned, from a connected seller account. This page ranks what one item you have not listed yet would net across six channels — free, in your browser, with nothing connected.

What each product is for

Sellerboard is a paid analytics subscription that connects to a seller account and reports profit and loss on orders that have already happened. Its subject matter is settled reality: real orders, real fees as the marketplace actually charged them, refunds, returns, advertising spend, cost of goods, reconciled per SKU and kept current as the account changes. It is built for a seller who is already selling and needs to know what the business earned, which SKUs are quietly losing money, and where the margin went.

This page does none of that. It connects to nothing, has no account, no login, and no memory between visits. It takes one item you are still deciding about — price, landed cost, category, monthly volume — applies each channel's published fee structure, and ranks the resulting net profit across eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop, and your own store side by side. Its subject matter is a decision you have not made yet, on channels you may have never sold on, which is precisely the case no history can answer.

What you want to knowWhere to answer it
What did my shipped orders actually earn last month, after real fees, refunds and ad spend?Sellerboard or comparable connected analytics — that is settled data this page never sees.
I am holding one item. Which of six channels nets me the most if I list it there?This tool — type it once, see all six ranked, free and instantly.
Which of my existing SKUs is quietly losing money once returns and advertising are counted?Sellerboard — that needs your real order history reconciled per SKU.
What would this item net on a marketplace I have never sold on and have no account with?This tool — it needs no account anywhere, so an unfamiliar channel ranks beside the familiar ones.
At what price does this item break even on each channel?This tool — it prints a per-channel break-even price from the cost you typed.
Do I have to connect a seller account, or upload anything, to use it?This tool: no. Sellerboard connects to your seller account by design, because that is where the data it reports lives.

A seller can reasonably want both, and many will: connected analytics for the business that exists, and a free local comparison for the listing decision that has not been made. They are not competing answers to one question. This page makes no claim about Sellerboard's accuracy, features, or current terms, and does not evaluate it — it describes only the shape of the product, as Sellerboard describes it publicly, and states what this tool does differently.

No account and no sign-in: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

What this tool cannot tell you

Worth being blunt about, because it is the honest half of the comparison above. This page never sees a real order, so every figure it prints is arithmetic on what you typed:

  • The fee rates are editable defaults, not a live fee schedule. They were current when the page was written. Marketplaces change them. Confirm against your own statement before pricing a catalogue.
  • It does not know your refunds, returns, or advertising spend. A channel that ranks first here can finish last once those land, and only connected analytics will show you that.
  • It does not know your negotiated or account-specific rates, your actual referral category as the marketplace classifies it, or promotional rates you are enrolled in.
  • Your own store almost always tops the table on arithmetic, and that is the least useful row. It charges no referral fee, but it also sends you nobody. Read it as "what I keep on a sale I brought myself", and weigh the cost of bringing it.

Those limits are the reason the comparison above is a comparison of shapes rather than a claim that one product replaces the other.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or Sellerboard?

They answer different questions, at different points in time. Sellerboard is a paid analytics subscription that connects to a seller account and reports profit and loss on orders that have already happened: real settlement data, real refunds, real advertising spend, reconciled per SKU and updated as your account does. This page has no account connection and no history. It takes one item you are still deciding about, applies each channel's published fee structure to the price and landed cost you type, and ranks the resulting net profit across eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop, and your own store side by side. A seller who wants to know what their business actually earned last month is asking Sellerboard's question. A seller holding an item and deciding where to list it is asking this page's question, and no amount of history answers it for a channel they have never sold on.

Can this page replace connected seller analytics?

No, and it does not try to. It never sees a real order. Every figure it prints is arithmetic on the numbers you typed and the fee rates shown on the page, which are editable defaults rather than a live fee schedule, so it cannot know your actual referral category, your negotiated rates, your refund rate, your ad spend, or what a marketplace actually settled to you. Confirm any rate against your own statement before pricing a catalogue against it. What it does instead is work before there is anything to reconcile, on a channel you have no account with, without connecting anything.

Is this page affiliated with Sellerboard?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Sellerboard. Sellerboard is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Sellerboard's own public description of its product.

Use it safely

which-marketplace-has-the-lowest-fees.ht.text:
Which marketplace has the lowest fees?

The short answer is that there isn't one. The cheapest channel changes with what you sell, and on two of the biggest marketplaces it changes by a factor of two and a half. Here is the arithmetic.

Compare your own item →

The flat-rate channels

Three of the six charge the same percentage whatever you sell:

  • TikTok Shop — about 6% US referral on most categories.
  • Etsy — 6.5% transaction plus about 3% payment processing, so roughly 9.5%, plus a $0.20 listing fee and $0.25 per payment.
  • eBay — about 13.6% final value fee plus $0.40 per order.

If those were the only three, the ranking would never move and this page would not need to exist.

The category channels are where it flips

Amazon and Walmart charge a referral fee set by category. On the same $40 item, with the same $18 of landed cost:

Channel Total fees, electronics Total fees, jewelry
TikTok Shop (6%)$2.40$2.40
Walmart (8% / 20%)$3.20$8.00
Amazon (8% / 20%)$4.00$8.80
Etsy (9.5%)$4.25$4.25
eBay (13.6%)$5.84$5.84

Totals, not just the percentage: eBay's $0.40 per order and Etsy's $0.20 listing plus $0.25 payment fee are included, and Amazon's $39.99 monthly plan is spread over 50 orders a month at $0.80 each. Change the volume and the Amazon row moves.

On electronics, Amazon costs $1.84 an order less than eBay. On jewelry, it costs $2.96 more than eBay for the identical sale — and $4.55 more than Etsy, which was the more expensive of the two on electronics. A seller who learned "Amazon is cheaper" from an electronics listing and carried that to a jewelry listing has it backwards.

Three things that quietly move the answer

The fee is charged on shipping too. On every marketplace here, the percentage applies to the whole order — the item price plus any shipping the buyer paid. Folding postage into the price to advertise free shipping does not dodge it. A $35 item with $5 shipping and a $40 item with free shipping pay exactly the same fee.

Subscriptions are real money at low volume. Amazon's Professional plan is $39.99 a month and a Shopify Basic store is $39. At 100 orders a month that is 40 cents an order and barely matters. At 4 orders a month it is $10 an order and dominates every percentage on this page. The comparison asks for your order volume for exactly this reason.

The cheapest channel may send you nobody. Your own store pays payment processing of roughly 2.9% plus 30 cents and no referral fee at all, so on arithmetic it wins almost every comparison. But a marketplace fee is not a tax — it is what you pay for buyers who are already there. Your own store's higher net profit only exists on a sale you brought yourself, and the advertising that brings it is a cost no fee calculator can see.

What a headline rate cannot tell you

Each channel has a second layer this comparison deliberately leaves out, because it depends on the listing rather than the fee schedule:

  • Amazon FBA fulfilment and storage, which turn on size tier and weight.
  • Etsy Offsite Ads, which take another 12–15% on the orders they fire on.
  • eBay Promoted Listings, where the rate is whatever you bid.
  • TikTok creator commission, and the announced October 2026 move to 8% plus 1.5% facilitation.
  • Shopify plan tiers, where a higher monthly fee buys a lower transaction rate.
  • Walmart WFS fulfilment and storage.

Selling wholesale rather than retail is a different question again — see the Faire wholesale calculator.

Livestream auction fees are a different question again — commission on the hammer and processing on the checkout total, with category caps — see the Whatnot seller payout calculator.

Run the comparison on your item →

Fee rates quoted here were current when this page was written and are starting points, not a live fee schedule. Confirm against your own statement before pricing a catalogue against them.
